text:
Last Year's Top Performing ETFs Still On A Roll 

Similar to the internal combustion engine, electricity and the telephone in the late 1800s, says ARK Invest founder, CEO and CIO Catherine Wood, today's innovations like artificial intelligence, blockchain technology and robotics are breaking new ground. 
Before starting ARK Investment Management in 2014, Wood served for 12 years as chief investment officer of Global Thematic Strategies at AllianceBernstein, where she managed more than $5 billion. Prior to that, she co-founded hedge fund Tupelo Capital Management, which managed $800 million in global thematic strategies. 
We touched base with Wood as ARKK and ARKW wrapped up 2017 among the top sector funds. They've continued to outperform the broader market this year with respective gains of 7% and 9% through Jan. 16, vs. 4% for the S&P 500. 
The full interview with Wood follows: 
IBD: Congratulations on the three-year anniversary of the four ARK actively managed ETFs. Have they performed to your expectations? 
Wood: Thank you for your kind words! Our aim for each of the funds is a total return of 15% on average, or a doubling, over five years. After a little more than three years, ARKK and ARKW are outpacing that goal significantly. ARKQ also is ahead of that pace, though less so (average annual gains the past three years 27.03%, 37.05% and 25.04% respectively), and ARKG is lagging (4.13%) primarily because of the pre- and postelection rhetoric around pricing in the health care sector. 
IBD: ARKK and ARKW were among 2017's top performers. What do you think helped drive their performance? 
Wood: GBTC, the Bitcoin Investment Trust, contributed more than 25 percentage points of performance to each, but the balance of the outperformance relative to the MSCI World (index) was broad-based, as investors began to extend their investment time horizons to gain exposure to the innovation platforms that are beginning to change their lives. Blockchain technology is one platform, but ARKW also is currently focused on the next-generation internet (artificial intelligence and connected mobile devices). ARKK currently has exposure not only to those platforms, but also to genomic sequencing, robotics and energy storage (electric vehicles). 
IBD: Both ETFs hold Bitcoin Investment Trust. What are your thoughts on Bitcoin and its explosive gains last year? How high — or low — can Bitcoin go? 
Wood: ARKK and ARKW were the first ETFs to gain exposure to Bitcoin through investment in GBTC when it was selling at less than $250 in September 2015. Today, it is approaching $17,000 per coin (near $10,235 as of Jan. 17). At $300 billion in network value, Bitcoin is selling at roughly a third of the market cap of Apple ( AAPL ), but it is a much bigger idea than Apple. It already serves the three roles of money: a means of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value, the last being its primary role at this time. The value of the monetary base is roughly $4 trillion and M2, $90 trillion. Bitcoin's $300 billion value pales in comparison. Beyond playing a role in the monetary realm, Bitcoin will become an important part of the move from centralized power structures to decentralized, distributed digital structures and services, including computing and supercomputing power, storage, and bandwidth, and social media. 
IBD: Robotics and artificial intelligence were big investment themes for the ARK funds last year. Do you see continued growth in those areas? 
Wood: Amazon rang the bell for robotics in 2012 when it bought Kiva. From 1,000 in early 2014, it has ramped to more than 80,000 robots in its distribution centers. At the same time its employment growth has compounded at more than a 35% annual rate and its organic local currency sales growth has accelerated to 29%. Teradyne is another important play on robotics, specifically collaborative robots, or cobots. We believe that automation will subsume lower value-add jobs while creating higher value-add jobs. On balance, we believe that robotics will be a net job creator. 
IBD: How do you decide what counts as disruptive innovation? 
Wood: Disruptive innovation is technologically enabled, creating platforms that transform economic sectors by providing greater simplicity, accuracy, customization and accessibility at lower costs. We center our thematic research on Wright's Law: learning curves or cost curve declines that drive rapid unit growth, productivity growth and wealth creation. 
IBD: In which other sectors or industries do you see disruptive innovation occurring this year — and/or in the future? 
Wood: Not since the late 1800s have we seen multiple innovation platforms evolving at the same time. From 1860 to 1880, three platforms — the internal combustion engine, electricity and the telephone — debuted. Today, five innovation platforms are evolving: genomic sequencing, robotics, energy storage (electric vehicles), next-generation internet (artificial intelligence/deep learning, connected mobile devices) and blockchain technology. In other words, technology is seeping into every sector, creating value traps in many of the stocks that dominate traditional equity indexes. ARK's funds are designed to offer a good hedge against the value traps created by disruptive innovation. 
IBD: How much weight, if any, do the overall market environment or economy carry in ARK's stock-picking decisions? 
Wood: ARKQ, ARK's Industrial Innovation ETF, tends to outperform our other ETFs when cyclicals are outperforming, so ARKK — which offers exposure to all of our innovation platforms and themes — will lean more into ARKQ's stocks in anticipation of a cyclically driven market. That said, all of our innovation platforms offer secular growth opportunities, regardless of the market's backdrop. Ironically, while they often underperform during "risk-off" markets, the fundamentals of these innovative companies typically gain traction as managements and consumers are more willing to consider change in order to cut costs, increase productivity, and introduce or try new products and services during troubled times. 
IBD: ARKG was up 49% YTD as of Dec. 6. What's driven performance there? 
Wood: Having spent eight years in Stanford University's biology research labs, four years in high school and four years in college, ARK Invest's genomics analyst, Manisha Samy, has steered us toward companies and stocks blazing a trail in the immunotherapy and molecular diagnostics spaces, with cancer a prime focus. We also have focused on the gene-editing space, aiming to capitalize on the companies that we believe have the most robust patents in that space, among them Editas ( EDIT ), Intellia ( NTLA ) and Crispr Therapeutics ( CRSP ). Based on Scott Gotlieb's stated objectives as head of the FDA and our focus solely on innovation, we have steered away from generics including biosimilars, which are facing increasing competition, and have focused on innovation and breakthrough technologies. 
IBD: Moving over to ARK's index funds, do you expect the 3D print industry to keep growing? 
Wood: Based on the research of one of our Industrial Innovation analysts, Tasha Keeney, the 3D printing industry is expected to grow 10-fold from $6 billion in 2016 to $65 billion in 2022. 
IBD: Let's touch on IZRL, which launched Dec. 5. Why do you think Israel is such a hotbed of disruptive innovation? 
Wood: It's in Israel's DNA, especially because the defense industry has been a hotbed of innovation. Israel has been dubbed "the startup nation" and is at the forefront of all of our innovation platforms. 
IBD: What do you think are some of the most promising companies in IZRL? 
Wood: Before launching IZRL, we owned a number of innovative Israeli stocks in our active ETFs. Among them are: Mazor Robotics ( MZOR ), Stratasys ( SSYS ), Elbit Systems ( ESLT ), Mellanox Technologies ( MLNX ) and Compugen ( CGEN ). We developed the ARK Israeli Innovation Index with this in mind, to capture and provide coverage to the most innovative industries and companies coming out of Israel — a very innovative collection of stocks that most investors have difficulty gaining exposure to. 
IBD: What inspired you to start ARK Invest? 
Wood: I created ARK Invest for two reasons. First, after the tech and telecom bust in 2000 and the financial meltdown in 2008, I observed that traditional asset management had become highly benchmark-sensitive. Benchmarks are backward-looking: They are where they are because of what has happened historically. Disruptive innovation is focused on how the world is going to change, something not captured adequately, if at all, by benchmarks. ARK Invest is benchmark agnostic. The second reason I created ARK Invest was to evolve an open research ecosystem, including social media and marketing, crowdsourcing, and thought leadership ("theme developers"). 
Determined to stay on the right side of regulation as a registered investment company, we added Chief Compliance Officer Kellen Carter to our team. Kellen served for four years at the SEC as an asset manager examiner and an attorney. During his tenure, the SEC was evolving its guidelines for social media and marketing. While many asset managers prohibit their employees from using social media for marketing, we believe that ARK Invest has a competitive edge as it is becoming a member of the communities focused on blockchain and other technologies that live on social media.
